articles.title: How many times has Israel violated the Gaza ceasefire? Here are the numbers
articles.description: Since the ceasefire took effect, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,439 Palestinians and injured 5,052.
articles.body:
Since the ceasefire took effect, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,439 Palestinians and injured 5,052.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info [Al Jazeera] By AJLabs Published On 11 Nov 2025 11 Nov 2025 | Updated: 2 Oct 2026 02:12 PM (GMT) Updated: 2 Oct 2026 02:12 PM (GMT) Since the declaration of a ceasefire in the Gaza Strip on October 10, 2025, Israel has violated the agreement with near-daily attacks, killing hundreds of people.
Israel violated the ceasefire agreement at least 4,379 times from October 10, 2025 to August 24, 2026, through the continuation of attacks by air, artillery and direct shootings, the Government Media Office in Gaza reports. It added that Israel had also detained 180 Palestinians from Gaza.
From October 10, 2025 to April 14, 2026, the office said Israel shot at civilians 921 times, raided residential areas beyond the “yellow line” 97 times, bombed and shelled Gaza 1109 times, and demolished people’s properties on 273 occasions.
Israel has also continued to block vital humanitarian aid and destroy homes and infrastructure across the Strip.
Al Jazeera has tracked the ceasefire violations to date.
On September 29, the United States unveiled a 20-point proposal to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, release the remaining captives held in the enclave, allow the full entry of humanitarian aid into the besieged territory and outline a three-phase withdrawal of Israeli forces.
Some of the main conditions of the first phase, which is ongoing, include:
Following mediation by partners including Egypt, Qatar, and Turkiye, representatives from some 30 countries gathered on October 13 for a ceremony to sign the Gaza ceasefire agreement, led by US President Donald Trump.
However, Israel and Hamas were notably absent, raising doubts about the summit’s ability to achieve tangible progress towards ending the war and resolving the core issues of Israel’s occupation and the 18-year-long siege of Gaza.
Israel has pledged not to allow a Palestinian state, and the US has continued its large-scale arms transfers and diplomatic backing to Israel throughout its genocidal war on Gaza, while offering only vague statements about Gaza’s future.
According to an analysis by Al Jazeera, Israel has attacked Gaza on 322 out of the past 358 days of the ceasefire, meaning there were only 36 days during which no violent attacks, deaths or injuries were reported.
Despite continuing attacks, the US insists that the “ceasefire” is still holding.
Since the ceasefire took effect at noon on October 10, Israel has killed at least 1,439 Palestinians and injured 5,052, according to the latest figures from the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
On October 19 and 29 – two of the deadliest days since the latest ceasefire – Israel killed a total of 154 people.
On October 19, accusing Hamas of violating the ceasefire after two Israeli soldiers were killed in Rafah, Israeli forces killed 45 people in a massive wave of air raids across the Gaza Strip.
Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, pointed out that Israel controls the Rafah area and it had no contact with any Palestinian fighters there.
On October 29, Israel killed 109 people , including 52 children, after an exchange of gunfire in Rafah that killed one Israeli soldier.
“The Israelis hit back, and they should hit back,” Trump told reporters, calling Israel’s attacks “retribution” for the soldier’s death.
On November 22, at least 21 Palestinians were killed in a spate of Israeli drone and missile attacks throughout northern and central Gaza, with dozens of others wounded.
Here are the latest figures from the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza, tracking the casualties from October 7, 2023, through October 2, 2026:
The ceasefire stipulated that “full aid will be immediately sent into the Gaza Strip”. However, the reality on the ground remains very different.
According to the Gaza Government Media Office, since October 10, 2025 to August 24, 2026 only 66,607 trucks entered Gaza out of 189,000. That is only 35 percent of the trucks allocated.
According to truck drivers, aid deliveries are facing significant delays, with Israeli inspections taking much longer than expected.
In addition, Israel has blocked essential and nutritious food items, including meat, dairy, and vegetables, crucial for a balanced diet. Instead, non-nutritious foodstuffs are being allowed, such as snacks, chocolate, crisps, and soft drinks.
On October 13, as per the ceasefire deal, Hamas released all 20 remaining living Israeli captives in exchange for 250 Palestinians serving long prison sentences and 1,700 Palestinians disappeared by Israel since October 7, 2023.
As part of the deal, Hamas is also expected to return the bodies of 28 Israeli captives in exchange for 360 Palestinian bodies held by Israel.
Israel has so far returned more than 300 Palestinian bodies, many of which were mutilated and showed signs of torture . Many remain unidentified.
As of December 26, Hamas had returned all 28 Israeli captives’ bodies.
According to the Lieber Institute, a ceasefire is designed to halt active combat, or “freeze a conflict in place”, but it can be ambiguous in international law.
The suspension of hostilities is best understood as a cessation of active hostile military operations.
Resuming hostilities would breach political agreements, but it might not be a violation of international law unless the ceasefire was part of a binding treaty or United Nations Security Council resolution.

articles.title: Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
articles.description: Flavio Bolsonaro beat polling expectations as Brazil’s right gained ground, setting up October 25 run-off with Lula.
articles.body:
Flavio Bolsonaro beat polling expectations as Brazil’s right gained ground, setting up October 25 run-off with Lula.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info This combination of pictures shows Brazil's president and re-election candidate for the Workers' Party (PT), Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (left), and Brazil's right-wing senator and presidential candidate for the Liberal Party (PL), Flavio Bolsonaro, during the presidential election on October 4, 2026 [AFP] By AFP , Reuters and The Associated Press Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is heading to a second round between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, prolonging a deeply polarised race with major implications for the country and the wider region.
Brazil’s electoral court confirmed on Sunday that the two candidates will advance to a run-off on October 25 after neither won the majority needed to secure the presidency outright, with Bolsonaro leading at 56 million votes to Lula’s almost 53 million.
Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades.
Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and is trying to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, even as the former president serves a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections.
While a second round was widely expected, the first-round result did not play out quite as pollsters had predicted.
Here are some of the key takeaways from the election so far.
With nearly 99 percent of votes reported, Bolsonaro had about 47 percent of valid votes, compared with 44.9 percent for Lula. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round.
That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro. This time, he will face the former president’s eldest son.
The race could be extremely close, as polling ahead of Sunday’s vote suggested Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro were roughly tied in a potential run-off.
That puts voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates in the first round at the centre of the fight for the presidency over the next three weeks.
Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who together received about 5.3 million votes, have previously said they will not endorse either candidate in the run-off.
Most polls leading up to election day predicted the race would be pushed into the second round, but had Lula finishing the first round ahead of Bolsonaro.
Instead, Bolsonaro emerged with a lead of two percentage points, raising questions about why the final polls underestimated his support.
On Sunday, Bolsonaro said the results showed that Brazilians want change.
Analysts told the Reuters news agency that Bolsonaro may have benefitted from “protest votes” from people who may have preferred another candidate but saw defeating Lula as the priority. Many had been expected to shift their support to Bolsonaro only in a second round, meaning this could have consequences for his support in three weeks.
“The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the run-off,” political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters. “While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded.”
After the results came in, Lula said the votes were “unexpected” but that he would come back stronger in the run-off.
“I admit, I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said.
Bolsonaro’s surprising performance in the first round was part of a broader show of strength for Brazil’s right.
Right-wing parties, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), were performing strongly in both houses of Congress, with the PL on track to emerge as the largest force in the Chamber of Deputies and making gains in the Senate.
This included victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family , including former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro, Flavio’s stepmother, who won a Senate seat in the Federal District, her first elected office.
His brother, Carlos Bolsonaro, was elected to the Senate in Santa Catarina.
The results show that the political movement built around former President Jair Bolsonaro – known as “bolsonarista” – remains a powerful electoral force, even with the former president barred from running himself.
“The fact that far-right candidates for the legislature have exceeded all expectations suggests a deeper popular grounding for the bolsonarista project than many expected,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera.
“Millions of Brazilians right now evidently feel the right best reflects their values and vision for the future,” he added.
The congressional results matter beyond election night, too. Both houses were already dominated by conservative lawmakers, and a stronger right-wing presence could make it even harder for Lula to push through his agenda if he wins another term.
A Bolsonaro victory, meanwhile, could give him more room to pursue his own priorities, including his pledge to seek an amnesty for his father.

articles.title: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez announces snap election amid housing crisis
articles.description: Sanchez calls an early vote after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
articles.body:
Sanchez calls early vote after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info A handout video grab made available by the Office of the Prime Minister of Spain shows Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announcing early elections for 29 November 2026, during a televised address in Madrid, Spain, 05 October 2026. [Office of the Prime Minister of Spain/ Handout via EPA] By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 | Updated: 6 minutes ago Updated: 6 minutes ago Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced a snap general election after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
Sanchez said on Monday that the vote would take place on November 29.
“We need to renew people’s support,” he said in a televised address.
“We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.”
He also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of previous campaign promises.
“I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today,” he said.
The government’s defeat in parliament on Friday was the latest in a series of political setbacks for the centre-left leader and was followed by mass protests across the country over the housing crisis.
The government said more than 70,000 people took part in a housing protest in the capital, Madrid on Saturday.
Anger had been building since late last month, when an 87-year-old woman, Marai del Carmen Abascal, was evicted from her home of 70 years in Madrid after an international investment fund bought her building and increased the rent.
But facing the electorate is a risky move for Sanchez. Opinion polls suggest that a coalition led by the conservative People’s Party (PP), with support from the far-right Vox party, is the most likely outcome in the election.
If they win, it would be the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco that a far-right party has entered central government.
If Sanchez loses the election, it would also mark the end of one of Europe’s last left-leaning governments as the far right continues to gain ground across the continent.
Sanchez has stood out worldwide for his strong stance on progressive ideas, from defending the rights of Palestinian people to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on tech oligarchs.
The prime minister, who has never won enough votes to form a majority government, has brought together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, ranging from the far left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms, lasting eight years.
The next election had been scheduled for next year before Sanchez brought it forward.

articles.title: Four African leaders issue joint declaration as Ethiopia war escalates
articles.description: Egyptian, Eritrean, Somali and Sudanese leaders also call for talks to end the civil war in Sudan.
articles.body:
Egyptian, Eritrean, Somali and Sudanese leaders also call for talks to end the civil war in Sudan.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Sudanese, Eritrean, Egyptian and Somali leaders pose for a group photograph during the quadrilateral summit in New Alamein City, Egypt, on October 4, 2026 [Handout/Villa Somalia] By Faisal Ali Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan have called for political and peaceful solutions amid escalating conflicts across the region, including Sudan’s civil war and major fighting in Ethiopia.
The leaders of the four countries – Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan – issued a joint declaration on Sunday following a meeting in New Alamein City in Egypt.
Ethiopia has accused Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of backing the armed alliance fighting its government. Officials from all three countries have denied involvement.
Earlier on Sunday, el-Sisi said that cross-border challenges required “a dialogue, not confrontation”.
The joint declaration appeared to push back against several policies pursued by Ethiopia in recent years, highlighting widening rifts between Addis Ababa and its neighbours.
The declaration backed Sudan’s military-led government and called for a political process led by Sudanese parties.
Sudan has been at war since April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Sudan and Ethiopia have traded accusations of interference in Sudan’s civil war.
The declaration also said control of the Red Sea should remain with the coastal states, seemingly in response to landlocked Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign access to the sea and a naval presence.
Somalia’s Mohamud told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Mogadishu does not object to Ethiopia securing commercial access through Somali ports, provided it is agreed with Somalia.
Egypt and Sudan, which have long disputed Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, warned against what they called “unilateral measures” that harm downstream states.
The joint declaration was issued as fighting escalated in Ethiopia between federal forces and a seven-group armed alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which fought a brutal two-year war with the government that ended with a fragile peace deal in 2022.
Government and allied forces retook the city of Mekelle on Sunday after the TPLF said it “temporarily moved out of” Tigray’s regional capital to “operate from somewhere else”.
According to Ethiopian state media reports, former Tigray interim leader Abraham Belay said on Sunday that the federal government is preparing a new temporary administration for the region and hopes to hold regional elections within months.
Ethiopian officials have accused neighbouring Eritrea of directly backing the rebel alliance in Ethiopia’s civil war.
Eritrea’s Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel said in a post on X on Sunday that Addis Ababa was trying to create a pretext for attacking Eritrea.

articles.title: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.description: IRGC commander says oil flows through US-supervised route in Hormuz are ‘negligible’.
articles.body:
IRGC commander says oil flows through US-supervised route in Hormuz are ‘negligible’.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Ships anchored off the coast of Khasab in Oman, near the Strait of Hormuz, on October 2, 2026 [AFP] By Reuters Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.
However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.
Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.
Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.
Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.
According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.
On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.
On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

articles.title: FBI arrests ‘Chinese foreign agent’ for spying on Taiwan president’s son
articles.description: A California woman allegedly sent photos and videos of President Lai's son and his family to Chinese officials.
articles.body:
A California woman allegedly sent photos and videos of President Lai’s son and his family to Chinese officials.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info US flags flutter over the entrance to the J Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, DC [File: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 The FBI has arrested a “Chinese foreign agent” at Los Angeles International Airport accused of spying on the Taiwanese president’s son.
Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, was arrested on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, Bill Essayli, said in a post on X.
Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te’s son, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a news article identifying him as Lai Ting-yu.
The US Justice Department said Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the behest of Chinese officials. She sent photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family to China.
Essayli called Zhang a “Chinese foreign agent” and said she “used tradecraft to avoid detection”.
“She never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense,” he added.
Essayli said Zhang will appear in a Los Angeles federal court on Monday.
William Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party say that Taiwan is already an independent country separate from China. Beijing views the island as Chinese territory.
Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself.
Earlier this week, the US delivered two F-16V ⁠Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China .
In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling Beijing’s long-held goal “unstoppable”.

articles.title: Samoa PM apologises after Nazi salute video emerges
articles.description: Pacific island nation’s leader says 2007 video showing him saying 'Heil Hitler' does not reflect his beliefs.
articles.body:
Pacific island nation’s leader says 2007 video showing him saying ‘Heil Hitler’ does not reflect his beliefs.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Samoa’s Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt has apologised over a 2007 video showing him using a Nazi salute [Courtesy of La’auli Leuatea Schmidt/Facebook] By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Samoa’s Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt has apologised after previously unseen video showed him leading a Nazi salute and saying “Heil Hitler” at a family gathering.
Schmidt issued the apology on Monday after the Samoa Observer, a local newspaper, published the seven-second clip the previous day.
The footage was recorded at a Schmidt family reunion on the island of Savai‘i in July 2007, when he was an MP and deputy speaker of parliament.
In the video, Schmidt is holding a microphone as he leads a “hip hip” exchange with the group before telling those present to raise their right hands and say “Heil Hitler”.
About a dozen people visible in the footage appear to follow him.
Radio New Zealand said it had independently verified the footage through its correspondent in Samoa.
Schmidt said on Monday that the words and gesture were inappropriate regardless of what was intended at the gathering and apologised for the offence they could cause.
“I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said, adding that the episode did not represent his beliefs or the values of Samoa’s government and people.
The apology followed criticism from academics contacted by the Samoa Observer.
Richard Evans, a historian of Nazi Germany, told the Samoa Observer by email that the footage was “shocking and disturbing”.
The paper also quoted University of Canterbury academic Anne-Marie Brady as saying Schmidt should explain and apologise.
Schmidt, who became prime minister in 2025, has made strong public expressions of support for Israel.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl at his swearing-in, where a shofar, a horn used in Jewish religious ceremonies, was sounded.
He has also pledged to open a Samoan embassy in Jerusalem before the end of 2026, a step taken by only a handful of countries because of the city’s disputed status and Palestinian claims to East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.
In his Monday statement, Schmidt said he considered the controversy addressed and would focus on the country’s economic and social challenges.

articles.title: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.description: In six decades of human spaceflight, only hundreds have left Earth, mostly men from the US and Soviet Union/Russia.
articles.body:
At least 746 people from 52 countries have been to space, from career astronauts to paying tourists.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Astronaut James H Newman waves during a spacewalk to connect the first sections of the International Space Station in 1998 [NASA] By Alia Chughtai Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title: Ethiopia’s forces retake Mekelle amid renewed Tigray fighting
articles.description: The capture of Tigray’s regional capital revives fears of another prolonged conflict, displacement and crisis.
articles.body:
The capture of Tigray’s regional capital revives fears of another prolonged conflict, displacement and crisis.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, has been retaken by Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters amid renewed fighting in the region [File: AFP] By Al Jazeera staff Published On 5 Oct 2026 5 Oct 2026 Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – The capture of Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle by Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters has revived painful memories of the 2020–22 Tigray war, with residents fearing a return to prolonged violence, displacement and economic hardship.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) confirmed on Saturday that it had withdrawn from Mekelle, saying its regional administration would temporarily operate from another location. Government forces and allied fighters entered the city on Saturday, with a pro-government militia source, a humanitarian worker and a Mekelle resident confirming to the Reuters news agency on Sunday that they were in control of the city.
The development comes less than four years after the Ethiopian government and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement that ended two years of devastating fighting.
Berihu, a 32-year-old bajaj driver in Shire, northwestern Tigray, said the latest fighting had been particularly difficult to watch.
“I feel very heartbroken knowing that Tigray has gone back to full-scale war,” he said in a phone interview with Al Jazeera. “We have already seen what the last war did to our people, and now it feels like we are going through it all over again.”
The 2020–22 war killed hundreds of thousands of people, according to estimates, displaced millions and caused extensive damage to infrastructure and livelihoods.
The African Union-facilitated agreement, signed in Pretoria in November 2022, ended the large-scale fighting, but key issues, including the status of disputed territories, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces, remained unresolved.
In July, the TPLF said the Pretoria agreement had effectively collapsed, accusing the federal government of failing to implement key provisions. The federal government rejected that characterisation, saying it remained committed to the peace process while accusing the TPLF of undermining the agreement.
The political dispute was accompanied by growing military tensions, including reports of sporadic clashes and drone strikes in parts of Tigray. The two sides also traded accusations over troop movements and preparations for renewed fighting.
The capture of Mekelle marks a major development in the renewed conflict, putting the city once again at the centre of the fighting.
In Addis Ababa, the developments have also alarmed residents who remember the consequences of the previous war.
Abel, a 30-year-old shopkeeper, said the fighting had felt distant until explosions were heard in the capital .
“I woke up and heard that my city had been hit,” he said. “You hear about fighting in Tigray, and it feels far away. But when you hear about explosions in Addis Ababa, you start asking yourself what will happen next.”
Diplomatic sources said explosions were heard in several parts of the capital, including near the headquarters of Ethiopia’s military. Reuters separately reported that a source linked to an opposition alliance claimed the group had carried out drone strikes in Addis Ababa, including against military facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.
For Abel, the economic consequences are as concerning as the fighting itself.
“If the war becomes bigger, ordinary people will suffer,” he said.
Bisrat, a college student in Addis Ababa, said the overnight explosions had reinforced his fear that Ethiopia could be entering a much wider conflict.
“If Ethiopia goes into a full-scale war, ordinary people will suffer,” he said. “I fear seeing another Sudan.”
Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when fighting broke out between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, displacing millions and creating a major humanitarian crisis.
The current fighting also involves a wider set of actors than the Tigray war that ended in 2022. The TPLF is part of a broader opposition alliance that includes armed groups from several parts of the country.
Fighting has also spread into Afar, while relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have sharply deteriorated.
Ethiopian officials have accused Eritrea of interfering in Ethiopia’s internal affairs and supporting forces opposed to the federal government. Eritrea has rejected the accusations.
On Thursday, Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, saying they had been involved in activities that posed a threat to Ethiopia’s national security.
Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia.
The diplomatic rupture has added to concerns that the renewed fighting could acquire a wider regional dimension.
In Mekelle, residents were left trying to understand what comes next after the TPLF withdrawal.
Goitom, 37, said there was a period of uncertainty after TPLF forces left the city, with what he described as a security vacuum allowing theft in some areas, including government offices.
“On Friday night, we were hearing gunfire but did not know what was happening,” he said.
By Saturday, Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters had taken control of key locations, including the airport, according to Goitom. Reuters and The Associated Press news agency also reported that government-aligned forces had entered Mekelle following the TPLF withdrawal.
“It feels like we are back to square one,” he said. “We have already seen what war can do to this city and to our families. People are worried about what will happen next.”

articles.title: Cornell case puts New York’s progressive image at odds with its rape laws
articles.description: New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including voluntary intoxication rule at the heart of Cornell case.
articles.body:
New York lawmakers will review sexual-assault laws, including the ‘voluntary intoxication’ rule at the heart of the Cornell case.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info A poster advertises an upcoming protest for sexual assault prevention at Cornell University in the US on October 1 [Lauren Petracca/Reuters] By Catherine Nouhan Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 Last month, a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, the fraternity Chi Phi and the seven fraternity members she accused of gang-raping her on the night of October 19, 2024.
Her allegations have triggered a nationwide reckoning in the United States over the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses.
But the case has also reignited efforts to reform laws in the state of New York.
While the left-leaning state has long presented itself as a leader in women’s rights, advocates say sexual assault survivors still face pervasive legal barriers when they seek justice.
Erica Vladimer, a lawyer and founding director of Harassment-Free New York, a survivor-led nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that much of the legislation currently in the spotlight is the culmination of years, if not decades, of work.
“These are bills that we have been fighting for for years when sexual violence is not in the news,” Vladimer said.
She drew a line between the #MeToo movement, which began in 2017 as an online campaign to denounce sexual misconduct, and the current wave of outrage following Doe’s allegations.
“It speaks to the fact that the #MeToo movement is not dead. It is a movement, not a moment,” Vladimer said.
Already, leaders in Albany, the state capital, have signalled they would take action following the Cornell case.
On Wednesday, the New York Assembly announced it had formed a working group to examine the state’s sexual-assault laws and develop recommendations for the 2027 legislative session.
Still, advocates say more concrete measures are needed to address the crisis.
“I appreciate that this work is happening,” said Lindsey Boylan, a New York City Council candidate. “It doesn’t undo the fact that rape culture is pervasive in the United States and very much so alive and well in New York.”
Boylan was the first woman to publicly accuse former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo of sexual harassment in another high-profile misconduct case, back in 2020. She is among those calling for greater reform.
Here are some of the measures advocates are pushing state lawmakers to adopt or amend:
The Cornell University case has brought renewed attention to New York’s “ voluntary intoxication ” statute, a legal loophole that can make it harder to prosecute sexual assault when a person has willingly consumed alcohol or drugs.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul pledged on Friday to work with lawmakers to close the gap.
“It should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.
Under the current state law, a person who voluntarily drinks or takes drugs is not considered “mentally incapacitated” during an assault, even if they become too intoxicated to consent.
That can make it harder for prosecutors to bring a sex-crime charge. The law primarily recognises incapacitation in the context of sexual assault when a person was involuntarily intoxicated, unconscious or otherwise “physically helpless”.
That distinction has become central to the Cornell case. Doe has acknowledged that she consumed substances before the alleged rape, saying that she was pressured into drinking alcohol and taking the dissociative drug ketamine.
The Tompkins County district attorney initially declined to bring charges, pointing to the law’s stance on “voluntary intoxication”. But the investigation has since been reopened, amid public pressure.
New York is one of 19 states in the US that distinguish between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication when it comes to determining consent in sexual violence cases.
But the Cornell case has spurred a push to remove the distinction from the law books. Critics have argued that sexual assault is no less grievous if a victim is drunk or has chosen to take drugs.
“I mean, to have New York, a supposedly progressive state, penalise people who are sexually abused for drinking is disgusting,” Boylan told Al Jazeera.
Vladimer, for her part, explained that distinguishing between “voluntary” and “involuntary” intoxication as a means for pursuing sexual assault cases shifts the focus onto the actions of victims, rather than perpetrators.
“We essentially have codified victim-blaming by saying if you become voluntarily intoxicated and then are sexually assaulted, you essentially cannot seek justice in our court system,” Vladimer told Al Jazeera.
In June, the New York state Senate unanimously passed a bill to allow sexual assault charges regardless of whether a victim is intoxicated voluntarily or involuntarily.
But the legislation has yet to be taken up in the state Assembly.
New York’s rape-shield protections limit the use of evidence about a complainant’s sexual history and conduct in criminal proceedings. But those protections do not currently extend to civil cases.
This distinction could matter in the Cornell case because Doe filed a civil lawsuit.
Vladimer said questions about a survivor’s behaviour could come up in the discovery process of a civil case, as well as in court.
“There is the potential of her having to face questions about things like her sexual history,” Vladimer said.
Bridie Farrell, the director of victim rights advocacy and legislation at the law firm Weitz and Luxenberg, told Al Jazeera that she has seen major differences in how male and female survivors are questioned in civil cases where this practice is still permitted.
In one case involving a brother and sister who were both sexually assaulted, Farrell said the man was not questioned about his sexual history while the woman was “grilled on

articles.title: Banned Bosnian Serb leader Dodik declares party victory in election
articles.description: Voters cast their ballots for a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government.
articles.body:
Voters cast their ballots for a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info A voter scans his ballot at a polling station in Sarajevo during Bosnia and Herzegovina's general election on October 4, 2026 [Stevo Vasiljevic/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP , AP and Reuters Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 The party of banned Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik has retained its grip on power in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s predominantly Serb Republika Srpska entity, with his ally set to keep the Serb seat in the country’s three-member presidency.
Preliminary results from Sunday’s general election showed Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), led by Dodik, ahead in the presidential race.
The result reinforced Dodik’s political influence despite his conviction and ban from public office, leaving a party that has repeatedly challenged state institutions in a strong position.
Dodik was not on the ballot after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy charged with overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian War.
Speaking to supporters late on Sunday, he said his party would not alter course.
“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said, while also praising United States President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory and thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin, a longtime ally.
Nationalist figures Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic, as well as leftist moderate Denis Becirovic, were leading the race as the Central Election Commission released preliminary results shortly after polls closed.
Becirovic, representing the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH), led the contest for the Bosniak seat. Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) led the race for the Serb seat. The Croatian Democratic Union’s (HDZ-BiH) Filipovic led the field for the Croat seat.
About 3.4 million people were eligible to vote in Sunday’s election to choose the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, legislators for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska.
Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.
The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric, and the division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former President Dodik told the final rally of the SNSD in the entity’s capital, Banja Luka, late on Friday.
In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
The European Union granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska, dominated by ethnic Serbs.
This general election is the first in the country to use new electronic tools to scan ballot papers and biometric fingerprint verification to reduce fraud.

articles.title: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.description: The abrupt redeployment to the US comes after several 'terrorism-related' arrests were made outside RAF Fairford.
articles.body:
The abrupt redeployment to the US comes after several ‘terrorism-related’ arrests were made outside RAF Fairford.
x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info United States Air Force personnel work on a B-1 bomber at RAF Fairford on September 28, 2026 [Alastair Grant/AP Photo] By Al Jazeera Staff , Reuters and The Associated Press Published On 4 Oct 2026 4 Oct 2026 The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.
Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.
Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added.
It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.
On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.
Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.
On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.
“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain – it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.
The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.
RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.
The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.
Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases, including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia, in March.
